setting_and_object.category: Algorithm (training framework) plus accompanying evaluation protocol/benchmark

details: Adaptive AI tutors need per-student feedback that is slow and costly to collect from real learners; existing student simulators satisfy only one of two needed properties: state-tracking/behavior-cloning models match a student's behavior but have no input channel for natural-language tutor guidance, while prompted LLM role-play follows guidance but fails to reproduce a particular student's competence.
Per-student learner data is extremely sparse (e.g., median 3 essays per L2 learner), so training one simulator end-to-end per student overfits.

StudentSim: a two-stage training framework that yields one individualized simulator per student — Stage 1 trains a domain base model on records pooled across many students (shared error patterns and the pathway from tutor language to a revised response), Stage 2 specializes that base on a single student's own single-turn and guidance-interaction records.

Formalizes per-student simulation as jointly optimizing two measurable axes: behavioral fidelity F (match the student's own response on held-out problems) and guidance responsiveness R (update toward the canonical corrected response after reading tutor guidance).
StudentSimEval: a standardized per-student evaluation protocol with frozen train/held-out record splits so any simulator family is fit and scored identically on F and R.

Three domains from real-learner corpora: chess (Lichess May 2025 human games; predict the player's next move in UCI), second-language English writing (EFCAMDAT error-coded subcorpus; generate essays matching a learner's error profile), mathematics (FoundationalASSIST/ASSISTments; predict the student's chosen answer recast as 4-way multiple choice with distractors from other students' real answers).

Every student has single-turn records (problem -> student response) and multi-turn records (problem -> wrong response -> tutor guidance -> canonical corrected response, e.g. Stockfish best move, EFCAMDAT teacher correction, audited answer key).

Roster of 60 students: 30 chess players, 15 L2 learners, 15 math students; chronological per-student splits; held-out sizes e.g. |S_i|=5,000 and |T_i|=4,000 in chess, |S_i|=26/|T_i|=40 in L2, |S_i|=66 in math.

Guidance modes mixed uniformly: chess (error remediation, comparative, strategic, Socratic), L2 (point-based, rule-based), math (error remediation, Socratic, conceptual); chess/math guidance wording is LLM-generated under fixed templates with the target response fixed in advance.
Chess F = top-1 move accuracy against the player's actual move; chess R = top-1 match to the engine best move after guidance.
L2 F = LanguageTool error-density similarity (total density plus mean over seven issue-type buckets); L2 R = normalized exact match to the annotated corrected fragment.
Math F and R = top-1 letter accuracy on the 4-way multiple-choice form (student's own recorded answer for F, canonical correct answer for R); population scores are means over students.
Base model Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507; LoRA (r=128, alpha=256, dropout 0.05, all linear projections) in both stages, bf16 on 8xA100 40GB via ms-swift.

Stage 1 pooled LoRA per domain with multi-turn ratio rho=0.2 (chess ~391 optimizer steps on 100k records from 100 players; L2 3 epochs on 7,800 instances; math ~91 steps); Stage 2 continues the same adapter per student at half the learning rate.
Greedy decoding (T=0), enable_thinking pinned False; headline numbers are cross-seed means over 3 full retraining runs.
Baselines: GPT-4o and GPT-5.4 prompted with student profile/problem/guidance; base Qwen3-4B-Instruct (L2 and math only); Maia2, a skill(ELO)-conditioned chess move predictor, for chess.

Ablations (chess): pooled Stage-1 vs. one student's records repeated to matched optimizer-step budget; text vs. vision (Qwen3-VL-4B with rendered board) input; sweep over multi-turn ratio rho; guidance-mode composition (leave-one-out, single-mode, Socratic weight scaling).

Tutor policy Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, SFT on rendered boards with grounding and hallucination filters, then GRPO (verl, 20 steps); all conditions share policy, SFT start, and GRPO config, differing only in reward.

Reward = tanh-squashed Stockfish (depth 15) centipawn improvement of the simulator's revised move over the student's wrong move; StudentSim condition adds two linear probe heads on the frozen simulator backbone (teaching-style gate, board-perception gate) as multiplicative gates.

Conditions: no-RL SFT tutor, GPT-5.4-prompted-simulator reward, pooled Stage-1 StudentSim reward; evaluated by competitive chess players (ratings up to 2200) blind to condition on accuracy, guidance quality (1-5), and personalization (1-5).

key_findings.finding: Trained per-student simulators are the only method strong on both behavioral fidelity and guidance responsiveness, while each baseline family fails on a different axis.
key_findings.evidence: In chess StudentSim reaches F=0.51, R=0.91 versus GPT-5.4 at F=0.23, R=0.72 (fluent guidance-following but poor per-student fidelity) and Maia2 at F=0.45, R=0.27 (decent behavior cloning but no input pathway for natural-language guidance, so R collapses near its zero-instruction floor); the same qualitative pattern holds in L2 and math, and StudentSim beats every baseline on F and aggregate R in all three domains.

key_findings.finding: Cross-student pooling in Stage 1, not just extra optimizer updates, is what makes per-student specialization work under sparse data.
key_findings.evidence: With Stage-1 and Stage-2 step counts, batch, LoRA config, schedules and seed matched, pooling 100,000 records from 100 players gives F=0.5131 / R=0.9003 versus F=0.4602 / R=0.8276 when one player's 1,000 records are repeated 100 times; the drop holds for each of the three evaluated players individually.

key_findings.finding: The gains are largest on the indirect guidance modes where the tutor never states the correct answer, indicating a genuine guidance-following capability rather than hint copying.
key_findings.evidence: StudentSim beats the strongest baseline on every guidance mode, including chess Socratic and math Socratic/conceptual; in a held-out Socratic chess case the 4B per-player simulator infers the engine best move f8b4 from a chain of questions while Maia2 repeats the player's blunder and GPT-5.4 picks the wrong queen square f8f4.

key_findings.finding: A trained StudentSim used as the RL reward produces a better chess tutor than a frontier-LLM-simulator reward or no RL, in expert human ratings.
key_findings.evidence: With tutor policy, SFT start and GRPO configuration held fixed and only the reward varying, competitive-player raters (blind to condition) score the StudentSim-reward tutor best on accuracy, guidance quality and personalization, while the GPT-5.4-simulator-reward tutor falls below even the no-RL baseline on accuracy due to a higher rate of severe factual errors; the style and perception gates are linear probes on the simulator backbone, which a closed API simulator cannot supply.

key_findings.finding: The training recipe is robust to the multi-turn mixing ratio and to input modality, and per-mode responsiveness is controllable through data weights.
key_findings.evidence: Chess sweeps show F essentially invariant in rho and R plateauing as soon as any guidance data is present (default rho=0.2 sits inside the plateau); a vision-language board-image recipe does not improve F over text-only FEN; single-mode training still yields R in [0.72, 0.80] versus 0.836 for the four-mode default, with Socratic hardest to acquire by transfer, and scaling the Socratic training weight scales its per-mode score in a graded way.
